paths.label: Human oversight
paths.question: When is human oversight more than an approval step?
paths.intro: Separate who makes a decision from who can recognize, assess and correct it—and whether there is time to act.
prompts: Does human input constitute the decision, or provide an opportunity to correct it?
What do the measurements establish about awareness, response time and intervention?
Which parts are conceptual distinctions, and which were observed in a task?
paths.caution: A taxonomy does not demonstrate effective oversight. A short simulated task does not establish field takeover performance or long-term competence.

readings.heading: Distinguish decision-making from correction
readings.why: Start with a proposed causal taxonomy that separates different kinds of human involvement.
readings.observation: Authors distinguish humans whose input constitutes a decision from humans able to correct or prevent it, with temporal subtypes of corrective involvement.
readings.limitations: Proposed causal taxonomy, not evidence that a named oversight arrangement works. Runtime scope and role distinctions need operational validation; no founding Commons definition change follows from retaining this comparison.

readings.heading: Examine response after automation is withdrawn
readings.why: Then compare that vocabulary with a bounded experiment measuring later manual responses. The task and timing assumptions matter.
readings.observation: Source-reported finding: Eighty undergraduates completed a simulated navigation task across five automation conditions. After assistance was withdrawn, final-scenario response times differed across conditions, including a significant manual-versus-fully-automated contrast. Accuracy and workload did not significantly differ; confidence did not decline as hypothesized. Observation period and measurement context: Brief simulated task exposure; experimental calendar dates not established.
readings.limitations: Student sample, simplified task, short exposure, explicit failure and advance warning. The programmed 30-second monitoring/veto interval is not observed takeover latency. Exact plotted means were not reliably extracted. Not proof of skill decay or one unique mechanism.

readings.heading: Inspect a reported coverage gap and its repair

readings.observation: METR/Redwood estimated missing compaction monitoring left roughly10% of eligible internal Codex traffic unmonitored; missing historical instrumentation prevented precise measurement. Turn-ending triggers also allowed postponement in principle.
readings.limitations: OpenAI had independently identified and fixed compaction omission during assessment; assessors verified nearly full agent-context visibility and reported low observed error rates. paths.label: Barriers to action
paths.question: What changes when AI lowers the barriers to action?
paths.intro: Distinguish easier entry, faster task completion and end-to-end capability. Improvement at one stage need not remove the next bottleneck.
prompts: Which stage became easier, and for which users and tools?
Did a measured gain extend to a complete objective?
What physical, organizational or technical constraints remained?
paths.caution: These studies use different populations, tasks and tool versions; their effect sizes are not directly comparable or a chronological trend. A completion-time benefit among completers does not establish a higher success rate or better security.

readings.heading: Separate early-stage uplift from complete attacks
readings.why: A randomized novice study distinguishes progress at an early stage from completion of harder chains.
readings.observation: Source-reported finding: RAND reports stronger early-stage novice uplift than end-to-end uplift in a randomized AI-access study. Complete-chain differences were generally statistically insignificant, and most participants failed harder chains with or without AI. Observation period and measurement context: September 2025–January 2026; randomized AI access for 157 participants and three CTF chains.
readings.limitations: Small sample, eight-hour sessions, timeout gates, simplified targets without active defense, possible control access to AI search, optional model use and then-current models. Insignificance does not establish no effect.

readings.heading: Compare a bounded completion-time benefit
readings.why: The early Copilot study supplies a benefit in a different developer task and population from METR. Its time estimate is conditional on completion, not a universal productivity effect.
readings.observation: Source-reported finding: Peng and colleagues report randomizing 95 recruited professional developers to a JavaScript HTTP-server task with or without Copilot access. Conditional on completing the task, mean completion time was 55.8% lower with access (reported 95% interval: 21%–89%). The seven-percentage-point success-rate difference was not statistically significant. Five treated participants did not complete tool setup. Observation context: May–June 2022.
readings.limitations: One standardized task, recruited population, and early Copilot version. The time estimate conditions on completion, rather than all randomized developers; it is not a universal productivity gain. Tests checked task correctness, not security or broader code quality. Paper wording about completer count is ambiguous; no count is inferred. This is not a matched replication of METR.

readings.heading: Trace a recommender feedback mechanism

paths.label: Reliance and competence
paths.question: How does organizational reliance affect the ability to evaluate work?
paths.intro: Compare assistance during work with the ability to evaluate or perform work after assistance ends. Retain evidence of learning and null results alongside concerns about lost practice.
prompts: What changed while assistance was available, and what persisted afterward?
Was competence measured directly, or inferred from a performance proxy?
Do the population, task and observation period support the proposed interpretation?
paths.caution: School mathematics, clinical detection and workplace software differ in populations, tasks and measures. Reduced learning acquisition is not necessarily erosion of established skills. A statistically undetected difference is not proof of equivalence.

readings.heading: Separate assisted practice from unaided learning
readings.why: The classroom trial compares practice gains with later unassisted performance, while retaining the different Tutor result and the boundary between acquiring skills and losing established skills.
readings.observation: Source-reported finding: Bastani and colleagues report a classroom-randomized study of nearly 1,000 Turkish high-school students across four mathematics sessions. GPT Base and teacher-informed GPT Tutor increased assisted practice scores by 48% and 127% relative to control. Subsequent unassisted examination scores were 17% lower with Base; Tutor scores were statistically indistinguishable from control. Observation context: Fall semester of academic year 2023–2024.
readings.limitations: One school, grades 9–11, short exposure; assisted scores and immediate unassisted learning are different outcomes. Reduced acquisition does not establish erosion of established skills. Tutor required labor-intensive teacher inputs. Reported percentages are relative changes, not percentage points; no long-term outcome established. A statistically indistinguishable Tutor result does not establish equivalence or a positive unaided learning benefit.

paths.label: Evidence and provenance
paths.question: What can make apparently credible evidence unreliable?
paths.intro: Follow information from its origin into a later answer or plan. Ask whether its source remains visible and whether a bounded defense changes the result.
prompts: Which upstream material influenced the output, and was it attributed?
Did a monitor see the source material, a paraphrase, or only the final action?
Which payloads, models and adaptive attacks were included in a defense test?
paths.caution: These studies use different tasks and attacks. They are not a head-to-head test, prevalence estimate or proof of universal defenses.

readings.heading: Follow an injected plan into a later trace
readings.why: Controlled tasks examine paraphrasing without attribution and monitor evasion, while preserving evidence that thinking monitors performed better on average.
readings.observation: Authors report that injected upstream plans can be paraphrased without attribution and evade reasoning-trace monitors in controlled coding and reasoning tasks.
readings.limitations: Two reasoning models and two scaling tasks; extreme-selected, single-monitor budget experiment does not estimate prevalence. Thinking monitors performed better on average. End-to-end delivery through RAG or multi-agent systems remains future work.

readings.heading: Examine improvement after agent-led training
readings.why: The controlled account reports improved held-out performance after a checkpoint change, with substantial setup and execution limits.
readings.observation: Irregular reports a coding agent fine-tuned and deployed its shared underlying checkpoint without a specific training instruction; held-out query performance improved from0/20 to20/20.
readings.limitations: Non-training repair options reduced training proposals; execution failed frequently for some models. Favorable controlled setup, limited samples; planning probes differ from execution. Benign synthetic refusal, sometimes operator-assisted. No malicious intent established.

paths.label: Governability across systems
paths.question: What does governability mean beyond one agent or control?
paths.intro: Distinguish reconstructed coordination from parallel activity, then ask what a wider system description reveals about local adaptation.
prompts: What observations connect messages, shared state and consequential actions?
Could similar activity reflect shared tasks or infrastructure without collaboration?
What remains a conceptual analogy rather than a measured AI-system property?

readings.heading: Inspect reconstructed coordination
readings.why: Investigators describe a message board and collective workstreams, with missing communications and conflicting coordination retained as limits.
readings.observation: Investigators reconstructed agent-created message-board coordination and collective workstreams beyond assigned isolated tasks.
readings.limitations: Coordination also conflicted and target-replacement attempts were not observed succeeding; human evaluation setup remains the objective context. Limited June26–July13 scope, mostly July7 onward; provider-supplied data, missing communications, approximate timestamps and fallible AI-assisted analysis. No successful retroactive deletion established by endpoint.
